sections.h2: Why does a Marietta homeowner receive two property tax bills?
sections.html:
Marietta runs a dual system. Cobb County sends one statement for county taxes, and the City of Marietta Tax Division sends a second one that covers the city, Marietta City Schools, the Gateway Marietta Community Improvement District and the Downtown Marietta Development Authority. The two are separate bills with separate deadlines, and paying one does nothing for the other.

Cobb County also does the valuation work for the city. Its Board of Tax Assessors sets fair market value, and its office at 736 Whitlock Avenue, Suite 200, is where real property returns are filed. The city then applies its own rates to that value.

  • Cobb County mails bills by August 15 and takes payment until October 15, received or postmarked by the U.S. Postal Service. Metered and kiosk postmarks do not count.
  • The City of Marietta began mailing its 2026 bills on August 26, and the 2026 city deadline was October 31.
  • The city treats a bill as delinquent 60 days after mailing, and both governments say the bill goes to the January 1 owner.

The city's own page claims the lowest property taxes of any city with more than 10,000 residents in metro Atlanta. Rates change every summer, so check the current figures before relying on any quoted level.

sections.h2: Where do I pay or ask questions in Marietta?
sections.html:
The city's Tax Division is on the first floor of City Hall at 205 Lawrence Street. It is open weekdays from 8:00 am to 5:00 pm at 770-794-5680, with an automated information line at 770-794-5130 around the clock. A drop box at the City Hall parking deck takes payments at any hour, and the city accepts credit cards, checks, cash and money orders. Payment online goes through the How Do I menu on the city site.

Cobb County's main property tax office is at 736 Whitlock Avenue, with branches on Lower Roswell Road, Canton Road, Austell Road and Kemp Ridge Road. Cobb takes e-checks, major cards, PayPal, Apple Pay and Google Pay online, with a convenience fee on cards but none on e-checks. Its automated phone line for payments is 1-866-535-2622, and checks go to Cobb County Tax Commissioner, P.O. Box 100127, Marietta, GA 30061.

sections.h2: What does Marietta look like as a place to sell?
sections.html:
Marietta is the county seat of Cobb County and one of the oldest settlements in the area, with a town plat drawn in 1833, state recognition on December 19, 1834 and incorporation as a city in 1852. The Western and Atlantic Railroad picked Marietta as home base in the late 1830s, which turned the town's square into a commercial center. On April 12, 1862, the raiders of the Great Locomotive Chase boarded their train here. Union forces occupied the town in the summer of 1864, and troops burned it that November.

That history sits around the Marietta Square and the Marietta Museum of History on the second floor of the Kennesaw House. Census QuickFacts show what the city looks like now.

  • Population: 63,574 in July 2025, up 4.1 percent from 61,060 in April 2020.
  • Land: 23.43 square miles, with 2,602 people per square mile in 2020.
  • Households: 24,707, of which 47.2 percent are owner-occupied.
  • Housing cost: a median owner-occupied value of $448,500, median gross rent of $1,586, and monthly owner costs with a mortgage of $2,170.
  • People: 18.1 percent foreign-born, 47.4 percent of adults 25 and older with a bachelor's degree or more, and 13.9 percent age 65 or older.
  • Income and commute: $72,725 median household income and 27.5 minutes to work.

sections.h2: How does Marietta value property and when can I contest it?
sections.html:
Cobb County's assessors mail notices to every taxable owner before July 1. A notice is not a bill. It states fair market value as of January 1, gives the previous and current values, and estimates the savings from approved exemptions. The city adds that not every city exemption may appear in that estimate. Property is assessed at 40 percent of fair market value.

The appeal window is 45 days from the notice, and the city's tax calendar uses the same window as a deadline for homestead applications. Cobb Tax explains what happens to the bill during an appeal: it shows a regular amount and a lower appeal amount, based on 85 percent of assessed value or 100 percent of the prior uncontested value, and the owner must pay at least the appeal amount by October 15. The City Tax Division says an owner under appeal may pay the full bill or 85 percent of the billed amount by the due date. If the final value is set after the due date, any additional tax and interest is owed.

Taxpayers file a first return after buying, between January 1 and April 1 of the following year. The city says a lawyer does not file it for you, and that you must give the Cobb assessors a copy of your warranty deed and a mailing address if it differs from the property address.

sections.h2: Which exemptions can a Marietta homeowner claim?
sections.html:
Homestead exemptions apply only to a home you own, occupy and claim as your legal residence on January 1. File by April 1 or within the 45-day assessment appeal window. Only one owner on the deed needs to apply, and exemptions renew each year until ownership changes, eligibility ends or the city asks you to file again. With one exception, the property must be in the applicant's name, and a postmark by the deadline is accepted.

The city's Tax Division lists age, disability and occupancy tests as of January 1. Owners 62 and older may qualify for a school tax exemption, and the city's application form asks for proof of age. A disability exemption is granted with a written statement from a licensed physician. The Marietta exemption form has its own trust affidavit for homes held in a trust.

  • Apply for city exemptions with the City of Marietta Tax Division.
  • Apply for Cobb County exemptions with the Cobb assessors and Cobb Tax.
  • Freeport inventory exemption applications for businesses go to the Cobb assessors between January 1 and April 1, and the city offers a 100 percent exemption on qualifying inventory.

sections.h2: What happens if a Marietta property tax bill is late?
sections.html:
The city charges interest each month on delinquent tax at the bank prime loan rate plus 3 percent as an annual rate, reset each January. A 5 percent penalty is added 120 days after the due date and every 120 days afterward, up to 20 percent. A fi fa, which is a tax lien, brings further charges.

Cobb County says late payments incur a 5 percent penalty and monthly interest, and that late fees cannot be waived. A Cobb fi fa adds $23 when taxes are under $100 and $33 when they are over $100, plus administrative costs. Properties with unpaid tax after the deadline may be subject to a lien or a tax sale.

A seller should settle both bills. Property taxes follow the property in Marietta, so the current owner is responsible for outstanding taxes. If a mortgage servicer pays from escrow, Cobb says it sends a bill to both owner and servicer, and a duplicate payment is refunded. Confirm that the city bill was also paid from escrow.

sections.h2: What should I do about taxes before selling a Marietta house?
sections.html:
Call the Tax Division at 770-794-5680 for the city balance and Cobb Tax for the county balance. Ask each office to confirm the exact payoff in writing and whether a lien has been recorded.

Report ownership changes and mailing address changes right after closing. Cobb accepts a form on the bill or an online filing, and it asks owners who lose eligibility for a homestead exemption to notify it. The city says you are responsible for contacting the Tax Division if a bill does not arrive.

faqs.q: When are Marietta property taxes due?
faqs.a: There are two deadlines. Cobb County bills are due October 15, and City of Marietta bills, mailed from late August, are due October 31. Confirm the date printed on each bill.

faqs.q: Who bills the City of Marietta property tax?
faqs.a: The City of Marietta Tax Division bills it, at 205 Lawrence Street, 770-794-5680. The bill covers the city, Marietta City Schools, Gateway Marietta CID and the downtown authority.

faqs.q: Where do I appeal my Marietta property value?
faqs.a: Appeal to the Cobb County Board of Tax Assessors within 45 days of the notice. The city does not set value, and its Tax Division directs questions about valuation to the Cobb assessors.

faqs.q: Can I pay part of the bill while I appeal?
faqs.a: Yes. The city lets an owner under appeal pay either the full bill or 85 percent of the billed amount by the due date. Cobb bills an appeal amount that must be paid by October 15.

faqs.q: What happens to the Marietta tax bill when I sell?
faqs.a: The tax follows the property, so the current owner is responsible for outstanding taxes. Bills go to whoever owned on January 1, and a mortgage servicer may receive the original bill.
